Q43089790.summary: Carved from a single piece of ivory, this comb has a fine row of teeth below an openwork field showing Christ on the cross, with a small titulus above, the Virgin and Saint John beside him and the soldiers with lance and sponge kneeling at the foot; half-length figures appear above the arms of the cross. Rosettes of openwork and curling acanthus fill the sides, and two figures bend among the scrolls at the top. Such combs were used in the liturgy, so that even a preparation for worship was set under the sign of the cross.
facts: The Museum Schnütgen holds the comb as inventory B 100; it is traditionally associated with Saint Heribert, Archbishop of Cologne (died 1021), though it was made more than a century before his time.

Liturgical combs of the 9th and 10th centuries were usually carved from a single piece of ivory and decorated with religious scenes, unlike secular combs; their exact use, perhaps at a bishop's consecration or before Mass, is unclear.
Q43089790.notes: Date and place (Metz, 850–900) come from the museum label as recorded in the Commons file title. Heribert's dates are general knowledge. The upper figures were not identified.

cur:catacombs-arles-orante-frieze.summary: A praying woman with raised arms stands at the centre of a crowded frieze in which Christ performs miracles among the apostles. The orans – the image of the soul in prayer – is placed literally in the midst of Christ's saving acts.
facts: The museum calls it the 'Sarcophage de l'Orante'.
Arles possesses the largest collection of early Christian sarcophagi outside Rome.
cur:catacombs-arles-orante-frieze.notes: Date approximate; individual scenes not verified.

cur:manuscripts-egberti-raising-lazarus.summary: Christ, with apostles behind him, raises his hand toward Lazarus, who stands wrapped in white grave-clothes in the opened tomb; Martha kneels at Christ's feet, and at the right the Jews, labelled 'Iudaei', lift the tomb slab, one of them covering his nose.
facts: Egbert gave the book to the church of St Paulin in Trier, where it was used in services until the 18th century; it has been in the Trier city library since 1810 and was added to UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 2004 with other Reichenau manuscripts.
Seven of its miniatures are attributed to the anonymous 'Master of the Registrum Gregorii', who worked in Trier.

cur:manuscripts-escorial-son-of-man-cand.summary: Christ stands with a cross-nimbus, a sword issuing from his mouth, holding a key, with seven stars beside him, and lays his hand on John, who has fallen at his feet; below, seven roundels bear the names of the seven churches. The tall, narrow panel distils the opening vision of the Apocalypse.
facts: The Escorial Beatus has 151 surviving leaves and 52 miniatures; it was probably made at San Millán de la Cogolla and was already in the Escorial library in the 16th century.
Its figures, with huge eyes and boldly patterned drapery, are among the most expressive in the Beatus tradition.
cur:manuscripts-escorial-son-of-man-cand.notes: Folio not stated on the Commons file.

cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: In a blue medallion, the haloed Christ sits blessing between two angels, above a many-winged cherub, while figures labelled with the names of the tribes stand below. The verse above calls on the Shepherd of Israel: 'thou that dwellest between the cherubims, shine forth before Ephraim and Benjamin and Manasses'.
facts: Its pictures interpret the psalms literally, historically or — very often — Christologically, as prophecies of the life of Christ.
The manuscript came to Württemberg under Duke Charles Eugene (its sale is first mentioned in 1787) and has been in the library at Stuttgart since at least 1818.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature.

vam:O92728.summary: This long, narrow ivory strip tells the story of Christ's birth as one continuous frieze: the Magi in Phrygian caps see the star and set out, the Christ Child lies in a manger in an open shed with the ox and the ass while Mary sits beside him, and further on the Magi hurry forward with their gifts to the Child held on his mother's lap. Rather than dividing the episodes, the carver lets them flow into one another, as on late-antique caskets.
facts: The panel is one of three in the V&A from a casket that was formerly in the Abbey of Werden in Westphalia; they were purchased from the Webb collection in 1866.
Scholars remain divided over whether the panels are Early Christian or Carolingian copies of Early Christian (perhaps 5th-century) models; the V&A favours a date of about 800.
The V&A links the group stylistically to a book cover in the treasury of Milan Cathedral and to related panels in Berlin, Toulouse and Nevers.
vam:O92728.notes: The V&A qualifies place and date with 'probably' (probably Lower Rhine, probably Werden, probably ca. 800).

Q500951.summary: A yellow crucified Christ rises from an autumn Breton landscape of orange trees and golden fields, while three peasant women in traditional dress kneel in quiet prayer at the foot of the cross. Gauguin used flat areas of bold colour and dark outlines to suggest that the women are seeing an inner vision, making the Crucifixion part of the living faith of rural Brittany.
facts: The figure was modelled on a 17th-century painted wooden crucifix in the Chapelle de Trémalo, a small chapel near Pont-Aven that still houses it.
The style, called Cloisonnism or Synthetism, was inspired by stained glass and medieval enamels, with colours enclosed by dark contours.
Gauguin later painted The Yellow Christ into the background of his Self-Portrait with the Yellow Christ (1890–91), now in the Musée d'Orsay.
The museum that owns it, formerly the Albright-Knox Art Gallery, acquired the painting in 1946.
